title: The Sketchbook in Drag, Parameterized: point, line, plane, family, balance, fall, swing, colour, and out
thesis: This course walks the way Paul Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook walks, the book Ada's own research plan says it wants to put 'in drag, in VR'. A point goes for a walk and becomes a line; the line closes into a plane you can stand on; the plane repeats and becomes structure; chance disturbs the structure and, given a memory, becomes ground; the body gets joints, becomes a family, stands, falls along a curve, swings, sounds and glows, and the book ends in colour. Where Klee stops, the course follows Ada's spine out of the sketchbook and says so. Every chapter also carries one of five verbs (repeat, transform, parameterize, visualize, simulate), so you can always say what your code is doing to form, and each verb needs the one before it: disorder is invisible without a grid, a family needs a class, a simulation needs all of these. The programming ideas arrive when a body needs them: a point needs a variable, a line a function, a walk a list, a floor a loop, a family a class, a balance physics, a curve your own gravity, a swing sine. In every chapter you build a body in GDScript, vary it along one axis, write down before rendering which two variants will look most alike, defend one sentence with the picture, ask what the approximation owes or hides, and then stand on the body, carry it, walk through it or become it. 'In drag' is not a costume here: Klee maps active, medial and passive onto brain, tendon and bone and onto male and female, and the scene tree does the same with parent and child. You will learn that hierarchy, and then make the passive end drive.

title: Bodies in Seven Verbs: a sketchbook in drag, in code
thesis: You start where Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook starts: a point that goes for a walk. You write an instruction, give a body a time, decide with one 'if' whether it is solid, carry it, join two points with a line, keep your walk, and close it into a floor you stand on. By the end of the first week a machine has drafted one of your bodies, you have caught it, and you are standing among made and scanned bodies in the headset. From there the parts are named by what code does to a body, so you always know where you are. You REPEAT a body until many become one, colour it by a rule, let a seeded draw replace the rule, give it noise to stand on and run one function for every pixel. You PARAMETERIZE it: the families you have been making by hand become a type with exported fields, a sheet in the editor, a budget and a file. Then you TRANSFORM it (joints, scale, a weather), put it under FORCE (a gravity you write, a balance that fails, a ray that reaches, legs that drive from the foot, a swing you hear, a game), let rules GROW it, and finally LEAVE THE LAB, where the approximations fail in public before you make a body others may change. Each idea arrives when a body needs it: a line needs a function, a walk needs a list, a family needs a class, a fall needs a force. The order is related to Ada's spine but not forced by it: chance, noise and colour come earlier than the spine puts them because you need them in the first month and because regularity must exist for chance to be seen; Parameterize has no spine place at all; every departure is named where it happens, and the spine index below shows each one as a jump. In every chapter you build a body, vary one axis, write down before you render which two will look most alike, defend one sentence with the picture, say what the approximation owes or hides, and take the body where a person meets it. One thread is queer in the code itself: the scene tree's parent-commands-child is Klee's active-and-passive chain, and later you make the passive end drive. That kind of geometric and bodily critique has almost no precedent in critical code studies; this course is trying it.

title: Walk, Repeat, Stand, Grow: a middle-ground course for Ada
thesis: This course starts where Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook starts: a point that goes for a walk and becomes a line, a record, and a plane you can stand on. Then one rule makes many bodies, a seed disturbs them, joints articulate them, a sine lays their time into space, and your body becomes a class: a family of possible bodies with one axis you can argue about. With a family in hand you give it surfaces (colour, tile, pixel, noise), then forces (the walker that carried you is opened, gravity is written by hand, legs let the passive part drive), then fields that decide what the picture hides, then rules that grow. It ends by leaving the lab: failure before futures, and your family placed in a shared museum where others may change it. The order relates to Ada's spine without being forced by it. Every chapter names the spine sequence it walks and is numbered inside it ('Randomness 1' at chapter 11, 'Randomness 2' at chapter 24, 'Randomness 3' at chapter 38), so you mostly walk Ada's halls in the spine's order. Where you meet a hall early, the chapter says why you need it now (chance right after the first grid, noise as your first ground, the model that drafts your code in week one), and when the sequence comes back, the chapter says it is a return. In every chapter you build a body, turn it into a family, write down before rendering which two members will look most alike, say in one sentence what the comparison shows, write what the approximation owes or hides, and put the body where someone meets it.

strengths: The clearest answer to Palle's ask, in one sentence a student can hold: 'walk the spine unless the student needs a hall earlier, and say so when you leave and when you come back'. Numbered returns (Randomness 1-3, Noise 1-2, Shaders 1-3, Parameterize 1-4) make the spine an index, not an order
The first self-moving body comes early and pays a debt left open on purpose: the organism at ch12 swings by sin with t += delta, repairing the frame-rate bug from ch2. Waves and sound follow at ch13

title: Assignments with a Lineage: what bodies are possible in code
thesis: This course is built like Golan Levin and Tega Brain's Code as Creative Medium: every chapter is an assignment with a lineage, a brief, one or two works from computational and conceptual art that answered it before you, a short closed exercise that trains one programming idea, and an open making step. What changes is the medium and the question. The medium is Godot and VR, and the question under every brief is Ada's: what bodies are possible? So each assignment asks you to build a body in code, turn it into a family along one axis, write down before you render which two members will look most alike and why, say in one sentence what the comparison image shows, write what the approximation owes or hides, and put the body where a person meets it: stand on it, walk through it, carry it, become it. The order follows the book's exercise ladder (graphic elements, iteration, colour, conditions, unpredictability, time, curves, simulation, learning, games), and it follows the Ada spine where the spine argues better: a Godot node is already a transform, forces come before waves, and the late crisis halls are critique beside code. Where the two disagree, the chapter says so. Chance and noise come early, straight after the tiling rule they disturb, because you need a regular pattern to see randomness, and they come back later as debt. The family (@export) comes early because every argument in the course sweeps one. Levin and Brain end their assignments with bodies (personal prosthetic, parametric object, public sculpture, extrapolated body); here you start with them.

title: Form+Code for Bodies: repeat, transform, parameterize, visualize, simulate
thesis: This course is ordered by what code does to form, not by the order of Ada's halls. First you learn what code is and make single bodies: a point, a line, a room you can stand in with the headset on. Then you REPEAT a body (a trace, a grid, a tile, disorder in the grid, a tree that repeats inside itself), TRANSFORM it (a pivot, a scale, an easing, time laid into space, a function turned into ground), PARAMETERIZE it (a class, a family in the Inspector, a budget you measure, genes saved as files), VISUALIZE what cannot be seen (a value as colour, a noise field, a shader, an implicit surface, a graph, a judgment), and finally SIMULATE it (forces, aggregation, balance, rules, soft bodies, swarms, navigation, learning) until the model meets what it cannot hold. Each verb needs the ones before it: disorder is invisible without a grid, a transform means most when there are many bodies, an argument about a family needs a class, and a simulation needs all of these. The Ada halls carry each step or are visited as field trips. Where this order leaves the spine's order the chapter says why, and where a topic comes back (chance, colour, recursion, graphs) it is a named return. In every chapter you build a body in code, vary it along one axis, write down before rendering which two variants will look most alike, and defend one sentence with the picture. Then you ask what the approximation owes or hides, and you take the body out of the lab into a place where a body meets it.

title: The Sketchbook in Drag: point, line, plane, balance, fall, swing, colour, and out
thesis: This course walks the way Paul Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook walks. A point goes for a walk and becomes a line; the line closes into a plane; the plane repeats and becomes structure; structure gets depth and must balance; the balanced body falls along a curve; what falls starts to swing, circle, spiral, sound and glow, and the book ends in colour. Kandinsky named the first three steps (point, line, plane) and Albers gave the method: every chapter is a controlled problem with a visible target, solved in one constrained material and compared side by side. You build each body in GDScript, give it parameters so it becomes a family, write down which two members will look most alike before you render them, and then stand on it, carry it or walk through it. The programming ideas arrive in the order the bodies need them: a point needs a variable, a line needs a function, a walk needs a list, a floor needs a loop, a family needs a class, a balance needs physics, a curve needs your own gravity, a swing needs sine. Klee never had randomness, noise, recursion or a headset. Chance enters where it entered his lineage, as disturbance of a grid you have already built (Nake's Hommage a Paul Klee, 1965). Where his book stops, the course follows Ada's spine out of the sketchbook and says so. 'In drag' means taking Klee's grammar seriously enough to re-assign it: his first part maps active, medial and passive onto brain, muscle and bone and onto male and female; the scene tree does the same with parent and child. You will make the passive part drive.

strengths: [V] Takes the 2023 application's own model at its word: Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook in drag. The point-to-line-to-plane-to-structure-to-balance-to-fall-to-swing-to-colour walk is a story an art student can hold in their head.

[V] The only candidate whose queer lens is a code lesson. Klee's gendered active/passive grammar is shown to live in the scene tree's parent-to-child command (ch12), then inverted by IK so the passive end drives (ch16).
[V] Ch7 'Plane: when the line closes' turns the recorded walk into a triangle fan you can stand on. The walk and the surface are one derivation.
[V] Albers's method as the argument strand, and Nake/Nees/Molnar to justify placing chance right after the grid (ch11).

anchor: Winnie Soon and Geoff Cox, Aesthetic Programming: A Handbook of Software Studies (Open Humanities Press, 2020; taught at Aarhus University's Digital Design programme): ten chapters, each pairing a programming concept with a critical theme and closing in a MiniX exercise with a RunMe (code) and a ReadMe (written reflection).
title: Aesthetic Programming in drag: bodies, code and debt
thesis: This course borrows its shape from Winnie Soon and Geoff Cox's Aesthetic Programming (2020): every chapter pairs one programming idea with one critical question and ends in a small work in two halves, the body you run (RunMe) and the argument you write (ReadMe). Here the work is always a body built in code, the argument is a family of that body with a prediction you write before you render it (which two will look most alike, and why), and the question is what the approximation owes. The order is the order in which you need things to make bodies. First one point that begins, resists, is held, is joined to another and leaves a trace (variable geometry). Then time and repetition turn one body into many and many vertices into a surface you can stand on (infinite loops). Then bodies come in from outside - a scan, your own tracked body, a touch - and the machine starts generating them by chance, noise, flow and rule (capture and auto-generation). Then you own a body type as a class, give it mass, balance and flesh, and let rules speak as recursion, grammar, sound and a recipe that travels (object abstraction and vocable code). Then the skin becomes data: pixels, shaders, patterns and fields (que(e)ry data). Last come the procedures that navigate, flock and learn, and the places where computation cannot close. Ada's halls are your field trips. The spine is the map you walk, but you will meet some halls earlier or later than the spine does, and each time the chapter says why.

strengths: [V] Its anchor, Aesthetic Programming, is the closest existing course in critical code studies, so it answers Palle's second question directly. A section maps what AP, Marino, Montfort, 10 PRINT, the Lexicon and CCSWG give, and says what Ada must invent: the body, the axis visible in a still, a falsifiable prediction, a geometric queer lens.

[V] Every chapter has one specific planted bug. Examples: i / N with integers giving hue 0; randomize() left in after seeding; one Resource shared by five bodies; CCW winding; add_child from a worker thread. For a beginner teacher this is the most usable material across all eight.
[V] The chapter anatomy table maps AP onto Ada: Decode = PRIMM predict in the hall, MiniX RunMe = body, ReadMe = argument, While() = debt, then peer feedback and pause weeks.
[V] Short track is the leanest: 9 chapters, 24 new ideas. It includes scan, player, chance, noise and class, and the mini-project brief is due as a flowchart on Friday of week 2.
[V] Forces come after classes (NoC's Mover) and chance before classes. Both orders are sound.
weaknesses: [V] AP's part labels are borrowed and sometimes forced. Fractals and sound under 'vocable code', or implicit surfaces under 'que(e)ry data', will not read as logical to a student.
[V] No small complete game or round. UI c15, audio c27 and save c28 never come together into a playable loop.
[V] Soft bodies are moved early because students have 'just written springs', but c22-c23 are an integrator and RigidBody joints, not springs. 2 departures are undeclared.

title: A Number Nobody Chose: bodies from chance, fields and rules
thesis: We start where the machine is least like you: with a number nobody chose. The first thing you type draws a random value and gives it to a cube; the second makes that value return, because computer chance is a pattern that repeats under a seed. Chance comes first because Palle's Queer 3D World, Ada's 2023 application and The Nature of Code all begin there, and because it hands your first body a debt you can see at once: the chance is computed. Chance is only visible against order, so the grid arrives in the same week (10 PRINT's 'regularity before randomness'), and noise follows as chance that remembers its neighbour: the field you will stand on. Only then do we go back to where Ada's spine starts, the point, the line, the face and the frame, because by then you have a crowd of bodies and a reason to ask where one of them is. From there the course runs close to the spine: forces, balance and waves (Klee's falling, standing and spiral), rules that grow (shaders, cellular automata, recursion, grammars, mazes), bodies that give, fuse, flock and learn, and the limits: impossible space, and entropy, where the first week's chance returns as a measure. In every chapter you build one body in code, make it a family, predict which two members will look most alike before you render them, say what the approximation owes, and put the body somewhere a body meets it.

[V] Closes where it opened: c36 brings week-one chance back as Shannon entropy inside QFEP, which is the application's arc toward entropy.

[V] The 'For the teacher' section is honest and useful. It uses a supplied-then-opened pattern (display.gd, walker, SKETCH, face_up), has planted bugs throughout, and its short track maps onto the Queer 3D format.

anchor: Palle Torsson's Queer 3D World course (Konstfack, three weeks, 2024 intro): the three layers of Ada Research, FOUNDATION (the lab), THE UNCANNY AND ALGORITHMIC DEBT, and ONTOLOGY (hybrid and impossible space), used as the macro-structure; scanned and sculpted bodies from week 1; AI-assisted code as practice; a mini project shown to the class.
title: Three Layers: bodies in the lab, bodies in debt, bodies out of bounds
thesis: This course is built like the Queer 3D World course: three layers, like an onion. Part I is the lab. You build bodies that hold still (a point, a line, a grid, a surface, a family of colours, a body type) and learn how each one is made. Part II is the uncanny. The same bodies start to move, fall, hang, sound, scatter and grow, and every one of those motions is an approximation that owes something: time chopped into frames, forces added up step by step, solvers that stop at 'good enough', chance that is only pseudo, noise that makes everything look like a blob, recursion that must be stopped, surfaces looked up in a table, models that learn their data's bias. Part III leaves the lab: your bodies are lost in generated worlds, go soft, grow skins, get cut and joined, swarm, become impossible from all but one eye, drift from order to entropy, and finally leave the computer as a build other people can walk into. Every chapter still passes through all three layers on a small scale: make the body, read its debt, give it a place. Your own scanned or sculpted body arrives on day one and comes back in every part, so the course is one body picking up a year of procedures. The order follows the Ada spine where the spine's order is the order your hands need, and says so where it does not: chance appears early as a value and returns later as debt, isosurfaces and machine learning close the debt part, and graphs follow the maze that needs them.

strengths: [V] The most Palle-shaped course. His own three layers are the parts, the student's scan arrives on day one and is carried all year (Zoog / Ecosystem), and the mini project 'the body the scanner could not see' reads like a real art-school brief.
[V] The short track is designed backwards from the mini project: every chapter is a step of it, with a day-by-day plan.

[V] Queer claims live at chapter level and are tied to code. c12: one integer parameter turns a pyramid into a cone with nothing in the class marking where. c36: a state machine is a list of allowed identities. c17: which body does the engine assume a player is? c01: who scans well is not neutral (stretchability, topology, bias).
[V] c27 turns the course's own AI assistant into the object of the bias study. c28's debt audit uses one quality export to scale every budget.
weaknesses: [V] Treating all motion as 'debt' makes the long track static for 15 chapters: delta at c16, player at c17. Beginners want things to move sooner.
[V] The first export is only at c37, the end of both tracks. That is late for a course that must ship to a headset.

[V] The short track leans on many supplied helpers (MeshDataTool displacement, shader template, CSG kit), with shaders in week 2. Students modify more than they make, and planted bugs are less systematic.

anchor: Geometry through code in an engine: Catlike Coding's progression (a graph of a function, mathematical surfaces, procedural meshes, pseudorandom noise, measuring performance), The Book of Shaders' order (shaping, colour, shapes, patterns, then random, noise, cellular, fBm), and Sebastian Lague's Coding Adventures as field trips: bodies from mathematics first, with the museum's halls as carriers and field trips.
title: Bodies from functions: geometry through code in Godot
thesis: Every body in this course is a function made visible. You begin with one point the engine keeps calling, then place many bodies by a function (a graph you can climb), then a field by a function of two numbers, then a jointed body that moves in time. You leave the grid for surfaces written as functions of (u, v), build the faces yourself, compare three ways of building one sphere, and turn your body into a family you can hold as a class. Next, light becomes a function (colour as a path, the first shader, pattern as symmetry), and only then chance, because a computer's randomness is also a function (a hash) and noise is chance that remembers its neighbours; this is the order in which engine and shader tutorials build geometry, and it is why randomness comes earlier here than in the museum. After that, bodies move by rules in time (forces, relaxation, oscillation, soft bodies), grow by rules applied to themselves (recursion, grammars, automata), appear from fields (marching cubes, carving), and choose (flocks, mazes, learning), until you reach where functions break (curved and impossible space) and the arc from order toward entropy. The museum's halls are where you see each idea at full scale; sometimes you visit them early, and each departure from the museum's order says why. Every chapter asks six things of you: build a body in code, make a family of it on one axis, write down before rendering which two will look most alike, make one comparison image and one sentence it supports, say what the approximation owes or hides, and put the body where another body meets it.

strengths: [V] One unifying idea, the dimensionality of the function: point, f(x), f(x,z), (u,v), mesh, shader, hash, noise, integrator, recursion, implicit, choice. It builds geometric capacity, which is Palle's stated core.

[V] The best visual arguments in the set. The five spheres (UV, cube, ico) at an equal ~320-triangle budget; hash quality from x+z to xorshift to full RNG (pseudo-randomness debt made visible); a loss landscape you walk down.

[V] Deepest engine craft (Catlike, Book of Shaders). ArrayMesh and packed arrays early, profiling early, a headless seed test, shaders as a returning strand, the XR rig and Quest preset by ch8, and a midterm game at c23 with the player opened on terrain at c21.

title: The Spine as It Stands: a braided course in the museum's order (control)
thesis: You will learn to program by walking Ada's museum in the order it is built. It opens as Paul Klee's point going for a walk and as the first semester every creative-coding course teaches: one body, a variable, a boundary, a frame, a measured relation, a recorded walk, a loop, a surface, a class, a pattern. Each idea makes a body you can stand on, walk through, carry or become. It continues as The Nature of Code: bodies that change, are thrown, balance, swing, happen by chance, fill space as noise, grow by rules, go soft, blur into fields, flock and learn. It ends where no coding course goes: graphs, the foundations crisis, the QFEP laboratory and the world outside the lab. Every chapter asks the same things. Build a body in code. Turn it into a family with one axis. Write down which two members will look most alike before you render them, then make the comparison image and one sentence it supports. Put the body where a body meets it. Then say what the approximation owes. This order is one choice among several: chance, noise and sound arrive late here, where The Nature of Code and Aesthetic Programming put chance early. The course keeps the museum's order so every hall you visit is the one you are learning in, and so you can see what the other orders would change.

strengths: [V] Opening (Day Zero to Point Trace to grid, triangle, smoothness, Melencolia) is creative coding's proven intro order, braided cleanly. Every chapter's debt and place is filled and specific.
[V] Museum as textbook: every hall a student visits is the hall they are learning in. That is a real practical advantage for a teacher.
[V] Ch2's debt is the best first lesson on time. Growing by += per frame runs 1.5x faster at 90 Hz than at 60 Hz, and the fix (delta) is held back to ch11 on purpose.
[V] Ch38 turns the student's own logged prediction errors into QFEP's F term (F = |prediction - observation|), so the course measures itself.
[V] Short track lists what is supplied and why. Export comes early (ch10), the player comes at ch12 and import at ch12.
weaknesses: [V] orderAgree 1.0 means the course is forced by the spine. That is exactly the audit-shaped feeling Palle objected to in the 115-stop plan.
[V] Chance first arrives at ch23. Before that, disorder is 'supplied' four times (Coordinates, Trans_Body, Array, Flow_Field): a ladder break the spine order creates.
[V] Odd placements: booleans at ch20 (conditions were ch6), threads at ch22 for sound, UI not until ch24.
[V] The queer lens stays in the debt notes. It never shapes a structural move.
